Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 85, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿By the sky containing the constellations,﴾ ﴿and the promised Day,﴾ ﴿and the witness and the witnessed,﴾ ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench,﴾ ﴿the fire fueled with fuel,﴾ ﴿when they were sitting over it,﴾ ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.﴾ ﴿And they did not resent them except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy,﴾ ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾

At the opening of the surah with this oath there is an arousing of eagerness for what follows it, and an indication of the importance of what is sworn to. Moreover, it draws the minds of the listeners to the things sworn by; for some of them are among the signs of the great power of God, which necessitates that Allah, exalted is He, be singular in divinity and that partners be negated; and some of them remind of the promised Day of Resurrection and point to the certainty of its occurrence, since an oath is only made by something whose occurrence is firmly established; and some of them, by what they contain of obscurity, direct the souls of the listeners to seek their explanation.

The relevance of the oath to what it is sworn upon is that what is sworn upon includes the lesson of the story of the companions of the trench. Since the trenches were lines made in the earth, ablaze with fire, He swore by the sky, with a qualifier from its attributes by which there appears to observers, in its stars, what the Arabs named "buruj" (constellations), and which resemble enclosures glittering with the lights of bright stars, similar to the blazing of fire.

Swearing by the sky with the description "containing the constellations" includes an oath by both matters together, so that the thoughts of reflecting people turn to what is in these created things and these conditions of evidence of the great power and the vast knowledge of God, since their creation according to those precisely determined measures is for people to benefit from them in the
صفحة ٢٣٨
timings of the months and the seasons. As He, exalted is He, said in something similar to this: ﴿That you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97].

As for the relevance of the oath by the promised Day, it is because it is the Day of Resurrection by the consensus of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil), since Allah promised its occurrence. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the Day which you were promised.﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 44], together with what there is in swearing by it of an incidental allusion to the threat against the people of the story upon whose content the oath is made, and the threat against their likes, who are indirectly referred to.

As for the relevance of the oath by ﴿the witness and the witnessed﴾, according to the differing interpretations of it, it will be mentioned when the interpretations are mentioned, and it is close to the relevance of the oath by the promised Day. Corresponding to it in what is sworn upon is His saying: ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.﴾

"Buruj" (sing. burj): it is applied to signs of the vault of the atmosphere in which it appears to the observer that the sun is in its position for a period of one month of the months of the solar year. So "buruj" is a noun transferred from the noun "burj" in the sense of a palace, because the sun descends upon it; or it is transferred from "burj" in the sense of a fortress.

The celestial "burj" consists of a group of stars close to one another whose distances never differ. It was named "burj" because the astronomers imagined that the sun stays in it for a period, so it is like a burj, i.e., a palace or a fortress. And when they found that each group of them could be imagined to form a shape which, if surrounded by an imagined line, would resemble the outline of an imagined image of some beings of animal, plant, or instrument, they distinguished some of those buruj from others by attaching to it the name of what that image roughly resembles, so they said: Burj al-Thawr (Taurus), Burj al-Dalw (Aquarius), Burj al-Sunbula (Virgo), for example.

These buruj are in reality sectors which the sun passes opposite in its orbit for a full month of the months of the solar year, by which they time the months and seasons through the position of the sun by day in the place where the stars of those buruj rise by night. This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqan: 61] in Surat al-Furqan.

﴿The witness and the witnessed﴾: both are meant as a category. "Al-shahid" is the one who sees, or the one who informs with truth in order to establish proof against its denier. "Al-mashhud" is the one seen, or the one testified against with truth. The object of the two descriptions is omitted, for the indication of the speech upon it. So it is permissible that "the witness" be the attendee of that promised Day from among the angels; He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21].

It is also permissible that "the witness" is Allah, exalted is He, and His saying supports it: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾ Or the messengers and the angels.

"Al-mashhud": the people gathered for the reckoning, and they are the people of deeds exposed to the reckoning; because the custom in gatherings is that the witness in them is the one spared its hardship, and they are the spectators who observe what takes place in the assembly, and that the witnessed is the one upon whom what takes place is observed by people.

It is also permissible that "the witness" refers to the witnessing angels, who are the guardians who witness the deeds, and "the witnessed" refers to the people of deeds; and that "the witness" is the messengers who convey to the nations, where the disbelievers say: ﴿No bringer of good tidings came to us, nor any warner.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19], and Muhammad (ﷺ) bears witness over all of them, and this is what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness over these?﴾ [an-Nisa': 41].

According to the various aspects, the relevance is evident between ﴿the witness and the witnessed﴾ and what is in the sworn-upon matter: His saying ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers﴾, and His saying ﴿when they were sitting over it﴾, i.e., present.

At-Tirmidhi related through the chain of Musa ibn 'Ubayda, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, the witnessed Day is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witness is the Day of Friday." That is, the estimate is: "and a day that is a witness and a day that is witnessed." At-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith we do not know except from the hadith of Musa ibn 'Ubayda, and Musa ibn 'Ubayda is weak in hadith; Yahya ibn Sa'id and others declared him weak on account of his memory." End quote.

Describing a day as "witness" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the meaning of this hadith is that this is among what is intended in the verse by the description "witness" and the description "witnessed"; so it is from the interpretation of the verse according to what the wording admits in both literal and figurative sense, as was discussed in the ninth introduction.

The answer to the oath is said to be omitted, indicated by His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ upon it

and the estimate is that they are cursed, as the companions of the trench were cursed. It was also said: its estimate is: that the matter is indeed true regarding the recompense for deeds, or "you will surely be resurrected."

It was also said: the answer is mentioned in what follows; Al-Zajjaj said it is: ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe.﴾ [al-Buruj: 12]. That is, the speech between them is a parenthetical interjection intended as preparation for the sworn-upon matter and an emphasis of the certainty which the oath conveyed, by mentioning the like. Al-Farra' said: the answer is "Destroyed were the companions of the trench," i.e., "qutila" is a statement of news, not a supplication nor an insult, and it is not necessary to mention "qad" in the answer, since the answer is in the past tense; because "qad" may be omitted, on the basis that its omission is not conditioned by necessity.

According to al-Farra's view, it is necessary that the statement be used in its necessary meaning, of warning to those who tempt the believers that there will befall them what befell the tempters of the companions of the trench; otherwise, a report about the companions of the trench does not need emphasis by oath, since no one denies it, for it is a well-known story among the Arabs.

The consistency of the plural masculine absent pronouns from His saying ﴿when they were sitting over it﴾ to His saying ﴿and they did not resent﴾ requires that the companions of the trench be those who set it up to torment the believers.

It was also said: the answer is the clause ﴿Indeed, those who tempted the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], so the speech between them is a parenthetical interjection and preparation in the manner we established in al-Zajjaj's statement.

His saying ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾: its form indicates that it is a formulation of an insult against them, an insult of disgrace and wrath; and these were not "killed," so the verb "qutila" is not a report but an insult, like His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the liars.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 10], and the saying: "qatalahu Allah" (may Allah destroy him). Its proceeding from Allah implies the meaning of cursing and indicates a threat, because wrath and cursing necessitate punishment for the act for which one is cursed.

It was also said: it is a supplication against the companions of the trench to be killed, like His saying: ﴿Destroyed is man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17]. "Killing" is used figuratively for the most severe torment, as one says: "Ahlakahu Allah," meaning He caused him to fall into the most severe hardship. In any case, the clause ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ according to this view is parenthetical between the oath and what follows it.

As for whoever made ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ the answer to the oath, he made the speech a statement and estimated it
صفحة ٢٤١
as: "Indeed, the companions of the trench were destroyed." Then what is meant by the companions of the trench is those who were thrown into it and tormented in it, and the word "ashab" (companions) is used in the sense of mere association and adherence, like His saying: ﴿O two companions of the prison﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. You have already known just now that the determination of this statement's interpretation is that the report is used in its necessary meaning.

The word "ashab" encompasses those who commanded the digging of the trench, those who directly dug and kindled it, and those who were in charge of throwing the believers into it.

This is a story about which the narrators differed in identifying it and in identifying what is meant by it in this verse.

All the narrations require that the people tempted with the trench were a people who followed Christianity in the land of Yemen according to most narrations, or in the land of Abyssinia according to some narrations. Various closely related narrations are mentioned, differing in brevity and detail, in sequence, in additions, and in identification; the most authentic of them is what Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from Suhayb that the Prophet (ﷺ) narrated this story to his companions. There is nothing in what was narrated explicitly stating that the Prophet (ﷺ) related it as an explanation of this verse, and al-Tirmidhi included its hadith in the exegesis of Surat al-Buruj.

From Muqatil: those who set up the trenches were in three lands: in Najran, in Syria, and in Persia. As for those in Syria, it was "Antyanyus al-Rumi"; as for the one in Persia, it was "Bukhtanassar"; and the one in Najran was "Yusuf dhu Nuwas." Let us mention the story which the Qur'an alluded to, taken from the biography of Ibn Ishaq, on the basis that it occurred in Najran in the land of Yemen. There was a king, who was Dhu Nuwas, who had a soothsayer or a sorcerer. The sorcerer had a disciple named 'Abd Allah ibn al-Thamir, who, when he walked to the soothsayer, would pass on his way a monastery in which was a monk who worshipped God according to the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and recited the Gospel, named "Fayminun," with fa', then ya', then mim, then ya' (it is vocalized in the European edition of the biography of Ibn Ishaq, which appears to have an original source vocalized as: fatha, then sukun, then kasra, then damma). Al-Suhayli said: al-Tabari has it with qaf instead of fa'. It may be distorted and said "Maymun," with mim at the beginning and one ya'. His origin was from Ghassan in Syria; then he wandered and settled in Najran, and he was isolated from people, secluded in his monastery. Miracles appeared to 'Abd Allah among his people, and whenever a miracle appeared to him, he invited those to whom it appeared to follow Christianity, so the Christians in Najran multiplied. This reached the king Dhu Nuwas, who was a Jew. The people of Najran were polytheists who worshipped a tall palm tree. So the king killed the boy and killed the monk, and ordered trenches to be made, into which wood was gathered and set ablaze, and the people of Najran were presented before it: whoever turned back from monotheism, he left alone, and whoever remained steadfast in the true religion, he threw into the fire.

So the companions of the trench were among those who were tormented from the people of the Christian faith in the land of the Arabs. Stories of trenches are numerous in history, and torment by burning is an ancient method, among them: the fire of Abraham (peace be upon him). As for the burning of 'Amr ibn Hind of a hundred men from the Banu Tamim and his being titled "al-Muharriq" (the Burner), I do not know that this was by means of making a trench. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: I saw in some books that the companions of the trench were al-Muharriq and his family, who burned a hundred men from the Banu Tamim.

The trench (al-Ukhdud): it follows the pattern *ufʿūl*, a form that is rare in use and not systematic. Other examples of it include *ufḥūṣ* (a hollow scraped in the ground), derived from the verb *faḥaṣat al-qaṭāh* ("the sand-grouse scraped the ground") and *al-dajājah* ("the hen") when she searches the dirt for a spot in which to lay her eggs. Other examples are *usluwb* (a noun meaning "method" or "a line of palm trees") and *uqnūm* (a noun meaning "the origin or essence of a thing"). This pattern may also occur with the feminine *tāʾ* (ة), as in *ukrūmah*, *ujūbah*, *uṭrūḥah* and *uḍḥūkah*.

His words "the fire" (al-nār) are a substitute (badal) for "the trench" (al-ukhdud), a badal ishtimal (a substitute of inclusion) or a badal baʿḍ min kull (a substitute of part from whole), because what is meant by "the trench" is the pit together with what is in it.

Al-waqūd, with a fatḥah on the waw, is the name of what fire is kindled with, such as firewood, oil or the like.

The meaning of *dhāt al-waqūd* ("full of fuel") is that its flame is never extinguished, because it has fuel that is thrown into it whenever it begins to die down.

The phrase ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾ is connected to the verb "was killed" (quttila). That is, they were cursed, and God's anger fell upon them, at the time they sat beside the trench.

The pronoun "they" (hum) refers to the people of the trench, since the king attends the execution of his command along with his chiefs, or it refers to those who were ordered by the king. According to the possibility that they were the king's helpers, "sitting" (quʿūd) means remaining close to the trench, which is expressed by sitting, so that those who stoke the fire do not become lax in keeping it burning. The preposition ʿalā (on/over) is used in its figurative sense of "over", because they did not sit above the fire but around it. The sense of nearness and watchfulness is expressed by the sense of "over", as in the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"The dew and the wind-blown one spent the night over the fire."

A similar usage is God's words ﴿he found upon it a community of people watering﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:23], meaning "beside it".

According to the possibility that "the people of the trench" refers to the believers who were tortured in it, then "sitting" is literal and ʿalā has its true sense of "on", meaning they were sitting on the fire, in that they were burning them while they were tied in the posture of sitting. That is because this is more severe in punishment and more humiliating. That is, after they had made them sit in the trenches, they lit the fire in them, and this is more awe-inspiring and more prolonged in punishment.

The pronoun "they" in His words ﴿and they are witnesses to what they do﴾ is repeated so that it is definitely understood to refer to some of the people of the trench.

The pronoun in "they do" may refer to "the people of the trench". The meaning of their being witnesses to what they do is that some of them bear witness for others before the king that none of them neglected what he had been charged with of burning the believers. Thus the plural pronouns and forms are distributed among different groups.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to what the context implies, namely the division of the people of the trench into rulers and subordinates, which is characteristic of great undertakings. So when He reported about the people of the trench that they were sitting over the fire, it was understood that they were the ones charged with supervising the workers. Thus it is understood that they had followers, from stokers and guards, and so they are the referent of the pronoun in "they do".

On this interpretation, "witnesses" (shuhūd) may be the plural of *shāhid* in the sense of one who reports a truth, or it may mean one who is present and observing, since it is evident that no one bears witness regarding his own action.

The clause ﴿and they are witnesses to what they do to the believers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾, as if it was said: "sitting, witnessing their action against the believers", according to the two possibilities mentioned above regarding the referent of the pronoun "they do". The benefit of this circumstantial clause is to make that sitting appear more horrifying and to magnify its crime, since they were watching the torture of the believers without showing any mercy or recoiling from it. By this, the content of this clause differs from the content of the clause ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾, in terms of the connection of His words ﴿witnesses to the believers﴾.

The use of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿what they do to the believers﴾ contains an ambiguity that conveys that the stokers of the fire, the guards, the workers and those who directly throw the believers into it displayed harshness and cruelty in torturing the believers, in humiliating them and in mutilating them, and this goes beyond burning.

(p. 244)

The clause ﴿and they sought nothing against them except that they believed in God﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The *wāw* is either the *wāw* of circumstance or a conjunctive *wāw* connecting it to the preceding circumstantial clause.

The intent is to express wonder at the injustice of the people of the trench, that they committed such atrocity, not for a crime that would justify taking vengeance against its perpetrator. If those who dug the trench were Jews, as was the majority of the people of Yemen at that time, then the statement is a form of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, that is, "they took vengeance on them for nothing that deserves vengeance, but rather because they believed in God alone, just as those whom they tortured believed in Him." The point of wonder is that King Dhū Nuwās and the people of Yemen were adherents of Judaism, so they believed in God alone and did not associate partners with Him. How then could they torture people who believed in God alone, like themselves?! This is similar to His words ﴿Say: O People of the Book, do you disapprove of us only because we believed in God and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:59]. If those who dug the trench were polytheists, then among the Arabs of Yemen there remained those who worshipped the sun. In that case the exception (istithnāʾ) is not from the emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, because the nature of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite is that what resembles the opposite of the intended meaning should in reality be of the same kind as the intended meaning. Therefore that device is used to emphasize the intended meaning. What is here is not like that, because the king and his army did in truth take vengeance on them for believing in God, if the king was a polytheist.

The application of the three attributes to the Name of Majesty (Allāh), namely "the Almighty, the Praiseworthy, ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾", serves to further establish that what they took vengeance on them for is not something that deserves vengeance. Rather, He is worthy of being praised for it, since they believed in a Lord who is worthy of being believed in, on account of His attributes which require that He alone be worshipped and that whatever is other than Him be rejected. For He supports His allies and rewards them, and He owns them. Whatever is other than Him is weak in might, neither harms nor benefits, and owns nothing of them, so the wonder at them is intensified by this.

The clause ﴿and God is witness over everything﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) containing a threat to those who made the trench and a promise to those who were tortured for the sake of God. It is also a threat to the likes of those disbelievers of Quraysh and others, to everyone who confronted the believers to harm them, and a promise to the Muslims who were tortured by the polytheists, such as Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb and Sumayyah.

A similar usage is God's words ﴿he found upon it a community of people watering﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:23], meaning "beside it".

According to the possibility that "the people of the trench" refers to the believers who were tortured in it, then "sitting" is literal and ʿalā has its true sense of "on", meaning they were sitting on the fire, in that they were burning them while they were tied in the posture of sitting. That is because this is more severe in punishment and more humiliating. That is, after they had made them sit in the trenches, they lit the fire in them, and this is more awe-inspiring and more prolonged in punishment.

The pronoun "they" in His words ﴿and they are witnesses to what they do﴾ is repeated so that it is definitely understood to refer to some of the people of the trench.

The pronoun in "they do" may refer to "the people of the trench". The meaning of their being witnesses to what they do is that some of them bear witness for others before the king that none of them neglected what he had been charged with of burning the believers. Thus the plural pronouns and forms are distributed among different groups.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to what the context implies, namely the division of the people of the trench into rulers and subordinates, which is characteristic of great undertakings. So when He reported about the people of the trench that they were sitting over the fire, it was understood that they were the ones charged with supervising the workers. Thus it is understood that they had followers, from stokers and guards, and so they are the referent of the pronoun in "they do".

On this interpretation, "witnesses" (shuhūd) may be the plural of *shāhid* in the sense of one who reports a truth, or it may mean one who is present and observing, since it is evident that no one bears witness regarding his own action.

How then could they torture people who believed in God alone, like themselves?! Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 85, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾

At the opening of the surah with this oath there is an arousing of eagerness for what follows it, and an indication of the importance of what is sworn to. Moreover, it draws the minds of the listeners to the things sworn by; for some of them are among the signs of the great power of God, which necessitates that Allah, exalted is He, be singular in divinity and that partners be negated; and some of them remind of the promised Day of Resurrection and point to the certainty of its occurrence, since an oath is only made by something whose occurrence is firmly established; and some of them, by what they contain of obscurity, direct the souls of the listeners to seek their explanation.

The relevance of the oath to what it is sworn upon is that what is sworn upon includes the lesson of the story of the companions of the trench. Since the trenches were lines made in the earth, ablaze with fire, He swore by the sky, with a qualifier from its attributes by which there appears to observers, in its stars, what the Arabs named "buruj" (constellations), and which resemble enclosures glittering with the lights of bright stars, similar to the blazing of fire.

Swearing by the sky with the description "containing the constellations" includes an oath by both matters together, so that the thoughts of reflecting people turn to what is in these created things and these conditions of evidence of the great power and the vast knowledge of God, since their creation according to those precisely determined measures is for people to benefit from them in the

timings of the months and the seasons. As He, exalted is He, said in something similar to this: ﴿That you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97].

Corresponding to it in what is sworn upon is His saying: ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.﴾

"Buruj" (sing. burj): it is applied to signs of the vault of the atmosphere in which it appears to the observer that the sun is in its position for a period of one month of the months of the solar year. So "buruj" is a noun transferred from the noun "burj" in the sense of a palace, because the sun descends upon it; or it is transferred from "burj" in the sense of a fortress.

The celestial "burj" consists of a group of stars close to one another whose distances never differ. It was named "burj" because the astronomers imagined that the sun stays in it for a period, so it is like a burj, i.e., a palace or a fortress. And when they found that each group of them could be imagined to form a shape which, if surrounded by an imagined line, would resemble the outline of an imagined image of some beings of animal, plant, or instrument, they distinguished some of those buruj from others by attaching to it the name of what that image roughly resembles, so they said: Burj al-Thawr (Taurus), Burj al-Dalw (Aquarius), Burj al-Sunbula (Virgo), for example.

These buruj are in reality sectors which the sun passes opposite in its orbit for a full month of the months of the solar year, by which they time the months and seasons through the position of the sun by day in the place where the stars of those buruj rise by night. This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqan: 61] in Surat al-Furqan.

This is a story about which the narrators differed in identifying it and in identifying what is meant by it in this verse.

His origin was from Ghassan in Syria; then he wandered and settled in Najran, and he was isolated from people, secluded in his monastery. This reached the king Dhu Nuwas, who was a Jew. The people of Najran were polytheists who worshipped a tall palm tree. Other examples are *usluwb* (a noun meaning "method" or "a line of palm trees") and *uqnūm* (a noun meaning "the origin or essence of a thing"). This pattern may also occur with the feminine *tāʾ* (ة), as in *ukrūmah*, *ujūbah*, *uṭrūḥah* and *uḍḥūkah*.

His words "the fire" (al-nār) are a substitute (badal) for "the trench" (al-ukhdud), a badal ishtimal (a substitute of inclusion) or a badal baʿḍ min kull (a substitute of part from whole), because what is meant by "the trench" is the pit together with what is in it.

Al-waqūd, with a fatḥah on the waw, is the name of what fire is kindled with, such as firewood, oil or the like.

The meaning of *dhāt al-waqūd* ("full of fuel") is that its flame is never extinguished, because it has fuel that is thrown into it whenever it begins to die down.

According to the possibility that they were the king's helpers, "sitting" (quʿūd) means remaining close to the trench, which is expressed by sitting, so that those who stoke the fire do not become lax in keeping it burning. The preposition ʿalā (on/over) is used in its figurative sense of "over", because they did not sit above the fire but around it. The sense of nearness and watchfulness is expressed by the sense of "over", as in the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"The dew and the wind-blown one spent the night over the fire."

A similar usage is God's words ﴿he found upon it a community of people watering﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:23], meaning "beside it".

That is because this is more severe in punishment and more humiliating. That is, after they had made them sit in the trenches, they lit the fire in them, and this is more awe-inspiring and more prolonged in punishment.

Thus the plural pronouns and forms are distributed among different groups.

So when He reported about the people of the trench that they were sitting over the fire, it was understood that they were the ones charged with supervising the workers. Thus it is understood that they had followers, from stokers and guards, and so they are the referent of the pronoun in "they do".

The use of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿what they do to the believers﴾ contains an ambiguity that conveys that the stokers of the fire, the guards, the workers and those who directly throw the believers into it displayed harshness and cruelty in torturing the believers, in humiliating them and in mutilating them, and this goes beyond burning.

The clause ﴿and they sought nothing against them except that they believed in God﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The *wāw* is either the *wāw* of circumstance or a conjunctive *wāw* connecting it to the preceding circumstantial clause.

The intent is to express wonder at the injustice of the people of the trench, that they committed such atrocity, not for a crime that would justify taking vengeance against its perpetrator. If those who dug the trench were Jews, as was the majority of the people of Yemen at that time, then the statement is a form of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, that is, "they took vengeance on them for nothing that deserves vengeance, but rather because they believed in God alone, just as those whom they tortured believed in Him." The point of wonder is that King Dhū Nuwās and the people of Yemen were adherents of Judaism, so they believed in God alone and did not associate partners with Him. How then could they torture people who believed in God alone, like themselves?! This is similar to His words ﴿Say: O People of the Book, do you disapprove of us only because we believed in God and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:59]. If those who dug the trench were polytheists, then among the Arabs of Yemen there remained those who worshipped the sun. In that case the exception (istithnāʾ) is not from the emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, because the nature of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite is that what resembles the opposite of the intended meaning should in reality be of the same kind as the intended meaning. Therefore that device is used to emphasize the intended meaning. What is here is not like that, because the king and his army did in truth take vengeance on them for believing in God, if the king was a polytheist.

The application of the three attributes to the Name of Majesty (Allāh), namely "the Almighty, the Praiseworthy, ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾", serves to further establish that what they took vengeance on them for is not something that deserves vengeance. Rather, He is worthy of being praised for it, since they believed in a Lord who is worthy of being believed in, on account of His attributes which require that He alone be worshipped and that whatever is other than Him be rejected. For He supports His allies and rewards them, and He owns them. Whatever is other than Him is weak in might, neither harms nor benefits, and owns nothing of them, so the wonder at them is intensified by this.

It is also a threat to the likes of those disbelievers of Quraysh and others, to everyone who confronted the believers to harm them, and a promise to the Muslims who were tortured by the polytheists, such as Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb and Sumayyah.

There was a king, who was Dhu Nuwas, who had a soothsayer or a sorcerer. Other examples are *usluwb* (a noun meaning "method" or "a line of palm trees") and *uqnūm* (a noun meaning "the origin or essence of a thing"). This pattern may also occur with the feminine *tāʾ* (ة), as in *ukrūmah*, *ujūbah*, *uṭrūḥah* and *uḍḥūkah*.

His words "the fire" (al-nār) are a substitute (badal) for "the trench" (al-ukhdud), a badal ishtimal (a substitute of inclusion) or a badal baʿḍ min kull (a substitute of part from whole), because what is meant by "the trench" is the pit together with what is in it.

Al-waqūd, with a fatḥah on the waw, is the name of what fire is kindled with, such as firewood, oil or the like.

The meaning of *dhāt al-waqūd* ("full of fuel") is that its flame is never extinguished, because it has fuel that is thrown into it whenever it begins to die down.

The phrase ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾ is connected to the verb "was killed" (quttila). That is, they were cursed, and God's anger fell upon them, at the time they sat beside the trench.

The pronoun "they" (hum) refers to the people of the trench, since the king attends the execution of his command along with his chiefs, or it refers to those who were ordered by the king. According to the possibility that they were the king's helpers, "sitting" (quʿūd) means remaining close to the trench, which is expressed by sitting, so that those who stoke the fire do not become lax in keeping it burning. The preposition ʿalā (on/over) is used in its figurative sense of "over", because they did not sit above the fire but around it. The sense of nearness and watchfulness is expressed by the sense of "over", as in the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"The dew and the wind-blown one spent the night over the fire."

A similar usage is God's words ﴿he found upon it a community of people watering﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:23], meaning "beside it".

According to the possibility that "the people of the trench" refers to the believers who were tortured in it, then "sitting" is literal and ʿalā has its true sense of "on", meaning they were sitting on the fire, in that they were burning them while they were tied in the posture of sitting. That is because this is more severe in punishment and more humiliating. That is, after they had made them sit in the trenches, they lit the fire in them, and this is more awe-inspiring and more prolonged in punishment.

The pronoun in "they do" may refer to "the people of the trench". The meaning of their being witnesses to what they do is that some of them bear witness for others before the king that none of them neglected what he had been charged with of burning the believers. Thus the plural pronouns and forms are distributed among different groups.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to what the context implies, namely the division of the people of the trench into rulers and subordinates, which is characteristic of great undertakings. So when He reported about the people of the trench that they were sitting over the fire, it was understood that they were the ones charged with supervising the workers. Thus it is understood that they had followers, from stokers and guards, and so they are the referent of the pronoun in "they do".

On this interpretation, "witnesses" (shuhūd) may be the plural of *shāhid* in the sense of one who reports a truth, or it may mean one who is present and observing, since it is evident that no one bears witness regarding his own action.

By this, the content of this clause differs from the content of the clause ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾, in terms of the connection of His words ﴿witnesses to the believers﴾.

The clause ﴿and they sought nothing against them except that they believed in God﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The *wāw* is either the *wāw* of circumstance or a conjunctive *wāw* connecting it to the preceding circumstantial clause.

The intent is to express wonder at the injustice of the people of the trench, that they committed such atrocity, not for a crime that would justify taking vengeance against its perpetrator. If those who dug the trench were Jews, as was the majority of the people of Yemen at that time, then the statement is a form of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, that is, "they took vengeance on them for nothing that deserves vengeance, but rather because they believed in God alone, just as those whom they tortured believed in Him." The point of wonder is that King Dhū Nuwās and the people of Yemen were adherents of Judaism, so they believed in God alone and did not associate partners with Him. How then could they torture people who believed in God alone, like themselves?! This is similar to His words ﴿Say: O People of the Book, do you disapprove of us only because we believed in God and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:59]. If those who dug the trench were polytheists, then among the Arabs of Yemen there remained those who worshipped the sun. In that case the exception (istithnāʾ) is not from the emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, because the nature of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite is that what resembles the opposite of the intended meaning should in reality be of the same kind as the intended meaning. Therefore that device is used to emphasize the intended meaning. What is here is not like that, because the king and his army did in truth take vengeance on them for believing in God, if the king was a polytheist.

The application of the three attributes to the Name of Majesty (Allāh), namely "the Almighty, the Praiseworthy, ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾", serves to further establish that what they took vengeance on them for is not something that deserves vengeance. Rather, He is worthy of being praised for it, since they believed in a Lord who is worthy of being believed in, on account of His attributes which require that He alone be worshipped and that whatever is other than Him be rejected. For He supports His allies and rewards them, and He owns them. Whatever is other than Him is weak in might, neither harms nor benefits, and owns nothing of them, so the wonder at them is intensified by this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 85, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿By the sky containing the constellations,﴾ ﴿and the promised Day,﴾ ﴿and the witness and the witnessed,﴾ ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench,﴾ ﴿the fire fueled with fuel,﴾ ﴿when they were sitting over it,﴾ ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.﴾ ﴿And they did not resent them except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy,﴾ ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾

At the opening of the surah with this oath there is an arousing of eagerness for what follows it, and an indication of the importance of what is sworn to. Moreover, it draws the minds of the listeners to the things sworn by; for some of them are among the signs of the great power of God, which necessitates that Allah, exalted is He, be singular in divinity and that partners be negated; and some of them remind of the promised Day of Resurrection and point to the certainty of its occurrence, since an oath is only made by something whose occurrence is firmly established; and some of them, by what they contain of obscurity, direct the souls of the listeners to seek their explanation.

The relevance of the oath to what it is sworn upon is that what is sworn upon includes the lesson of the story of the companions of the trench. Since the trenches were lines made in the earth, ablaze with fire, He swore by the sky, with a qualifier from its attributes by which there appears to observers, in its stars, what the Arabs named "buruj" (constellations), and which resemble enclosures glittering with the lights of bright stars, similar to the blazing of fire.

Swearing by the sky with the description "containing the constellations" includes an oath by both matters together, so that the thoughts of reflecting people turn to what is in these created things and these conditions of evidence of the great power and the vast knowledge of God, since their creation according to those precisely determined measures is for people to benefit from them in the

timings of the months and the seasons. As He, exalted is He, said in something similar to this: ﴿That you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97].

As for the relevance of the oath by the promised Day, it is because it is the Day of Resurrection by the consensus of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil), since Allah promised its occurrence. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the Day which you were promised.﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 44], together with what there is in swearing by it of an incidental allusion to the threat against the people of the story upon whose content the oath is made, and the threat against their likes, who are indirectly referred to.

As for the relevance of the oath by ﴿the witness and the witnessed﴾, according to the differing interpretations of it, it will be mentioned when the interpretations are mentioned, and it is close to the relevance of the oath by the promised Day. Corresponding to it in what is sworn upon is His saying: ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.﴾

"Buruj" (sing. burj): it is applied to signs of the vault of the atmosphere in which it appears to the observer that the sun is in its position for a period of one month of the months of the solar year. So "buruj" is a noun transferred from the noun "burj" in the sense of a palace, because the sun descends upon it; or it is transferred from "burj" in the sense of a fortress.

The celestial "burj" consists of a group of stars close to one another whose distances never differ. It was named "burj" because the astronomers imagined that the sun stays in it for a period, so it is like a burj, i.e., a palace or a fortress. And when they found that each group of them could be imagined to form a shape which, if surrounded by an imagined line, would resemble the outline of an imagined image of some beings of animal, plant, or instrument, they distinguished some of those buruj from others by attaching to it the name of what that image roughly resembles, so they said: Burj al-Thawr (Taurus), Burj al-Dalw (Aquarius), Burj al-Sunbula (Virgo), for example.

These buruj are in reality sectors which the sun passes opposite in its orbit for a full month of the months of the solar year, by which they time the months and seasons through the position of the sun by day in the place where the stars of those buruj rise by night. This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqan: 61] in Surat al-Furqan.

﴿The witness and the witnessed﴾: both are meant as a category. "Al-shahid" is the one who sees, or the one who informs with truth in order to establish proof against its denier. "Al-mashhud" is the one seen, or the one testified against with truth. The object of the two descriptions is omitted, for the indication of the speech upon it. So it is permissible that "the witness" be the attendee of that promised Day from among the angels; He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21].

It is also permissible that "the witness" is Allah, exalted is He, and His saying supports it: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾ Or the messengers and the angels.

"Al-mashhud": the people gathered for the reckoning, and they are the people of deeds exposed to the reckoning; because the custom in gatherings is that the witness in them is the one spared its hardship, and they are the spectators who observe what takes place in the assembly, and that the witnessed is the one upon whom what takes place is observed by people.

It is also permissible that "the witness" refers to the witnessing angels, who are the guardians who witness the deeds, and "the witnessed" refers to the people of deeds; and that "the witness" is the messengers who convey to the nations, where the disbelievers say: ﴿No bringer of good tidings came to us, nor any warner.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19], and Muhammad (ﷺ) bears witness over all of them, and this is what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness over these?﴾ [an-Nisa': 41].

According to the various aspects, the relevance is evident between ﴿the witness and the witnessed﴾ and what is in the sworn-upon matter: His saying ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers﴾, and His saying ﴿when they were sitting over it﴾, i.e., present.

At-Tirmidhi related through the chain of Musa ibn 'Ubayda, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, the witnessed Day is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witness is the Day of Friday." That is, the estimate is: "and a day that is a witness and a day that is witnessed." At-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith we do not know except from the hadith of Musa ibn 'Ubayda, and Musa ibn 'Ubayda is weak in hadith; Yahya ibn Sa'id and others declared him weak on account of his memory." Describing a day as "witness" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the meaning of this hadith is that this is among what is intended in the verse by the description "witness" and the description "witnessed"; so it is from the interpretation of the verse according to what the wording admits in both literal and figurative sense, as was discussed in the ninth introduction.

Its proceeding from Allah implies the meaning of cursing and indicates a threat, because wrath and cursing necessitate punishment for the act for which one is cursed.

In any case, the clause ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ according to this view is parenthetical between the oath and what follows it.

And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾

At the opening of the surah with this oath there is an arousing of eagerness for what follows it, and an indication of the importance of what is sworn to. Moreover, it draws the minds of the listeners to the things sworn by; for some of them are among the signs of the great power of God, which necessitates that Allah, exalted is He, be singular in divinity and that partners be negated; and some of them remind of the promised Day of Resurrection and point to the certainty of its occurrence, since an oath is only made by something whose occurrence is firmly established; and some of them, by what they contain of obscurity, direct the souls of the listeners to seek their explanation.

Since the trenches were lines made in the earth, ablaze with fire, He swore by the sky, with a qualifier from its attributes by which there appears to observers, in its stars, what the Arabs named "buruj" (constellations), and which resemble enclosures glittering with the lights of bright stars, similar to the blazing of fire.

His origin was from Ghassan in Syria; then he wandered and settled in Najran, and he was isolated from people, secluded in his monastery. It is also permissible that "the witness" is Allah, exalted is He, and His saying supports it: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾ Or the messengers and the angels.

"Al-mashhud": the people gathered for the reckoning, and they are the people of deeds exposed to the reckoning; because the custom in gatherings is that the witness in them is the one spared its hardship, and they are the spectators who observe what takes place in the assembly, and that the witnessed is the one upon whom what takes place is observed by people.

It is also permissible that "the witness" refers to the witnessing angels, who are the guardians who witness the deeds, and "the witnessed" refers to the people of deeds; and that "the witness" is the messengers who convey to the nations, where the disbelievers say: ﴿No bringer of good tidings came to us, nor any warner.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19], and Muhammad (ﷺ) bears witness over all of them, and this is what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness over these?﴾ [an-Nisa': 41].

According to the various aspects, the relevance is evident between ﴿the witness and the witnessed﴾ and what is in the sworn-upon matter: His saying ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers﴾, and His saying ﴿when they were sitting over it﴾, i.e., present.

At-Tirmidhi related through the chain of Musa ibn 'Ubayda, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, the witnessed Day is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witness is the Day of Friday." That is, the estimate is: "and a day that is a witness and a day that is witnessed." At-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith we do not know except from the hadith of Musa ibn 'Ubayda, and Musa ibn 'Ubayda is weak in hadith; Yahya ibn Sa'id and others declared him weak on account of his memory." End quote.

Describing a day as "witness" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the meaning of this hadith is that this is among what is intended in the verse by the description "witness" and the description "witnessed"; so it is from the interpretation of the verse according to what the wording admits in both literal and figurative sense, as was discussed in the ninth introduction.

The answer to the oath is said to be omitted, indicated by His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ upon it
صفحة ٢٤٠
and the estimate is that they are cursed, as the companions of the trench were cursed. It was also said: its estimate is: that the matter is indeed true regarding the recompense for deeds, or "you will surely be resurrected."

It was also said: the answer is mentioned in what follows; Al-Zajjaj said it is: ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe.﴾ [al-Buruj: 12]. That is, the speech between them is a parenthetical interjection intended as preparation for the sworn-upon matter and an emphasis of the certainty which the oath conveyed, by mentioning the like. Al-Farra' said: the answer is "Destroyed were the companions of the trench," i.e., "qutila" is a statement of news, not a supplication nor an insult, and it is not necessary to mention "qad" in the answer, since the answer is in the past tense; because "qad" may be omitted, on the basis that its omission is not conditioned by necessity.

According to al-Farra's view, it is necessary that the statement be used in its necessary meaning, of warning to those who tempt the believers that there will befall them what befell the tempters of the companions of the trench; otherwise, a report about the companions of the trench does not need emphasis by oath, since no one denies it, for it is a well-known story among the Arabs.

The consistency of the plural masculine absent pronouns from His saying ﴿when they were sitting over it﴾ to His saying ﴿and they did not resent﴾ requires that the companions of the trench be those who set it up to torment the believers.

It was also said: the answer is the clause ﴿Indeed, those who tempted the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], so the speech between them is a parenthetical interjection and preparation in the manner we established in al-Zajjaj's statement.

His saying ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾: its form indicates that it is a formulation of an insult against them, an insult of disgrace and wrath; and these were not "killed," so the verb "qutila" is not a report but an insult, like His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the liars.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 10], and the saying: "qatalahu Allah" (may Allah destroy him). Its proceeding from Allah implies the meaning of cursing and indicates a threat, because wrath and cursing necessitate punishment for the act for which one is cursed.

It was also said: it is a supplication against the companions of the trench to be killed, like His saying: ﴿Destroyed is man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17]. "Killing" is used figuratively for the most severe torment, as one says: "Ahlakahu Allah," meaning He caused him to fall into the most severe hardship. In any case, the clause ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ according to this view is parenthetical between the oath and what follows it.

As for whoever made ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾ the answer to the oath, he made the speech a statement and estimated it
صفحة ٢٤١
as: "Indeed, the companions of the trench were destroyed." Then what is meant by the companions of the trench is those who were thrown into it and tormented in it, and the word "ashab" (companions) is used in the sense of mere association and adherence, like His saying: ﴿O two companions of the prison﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. You have already known just now that the determination of this statement's interpretation is that the report is used in its necessary meaning.

The word "ashab" encompasses those who commanded the digging of the trench, those who directly dug and kindled it, and those who were in charge of throwing the believers into it.

This is a story about which the narrators differed in identifying it and in identifying what is meant by it in this verse.

All the narrations require that the people tempted with the trench were a people who followed Christianity in the land of Yemen according to most narrations, or in the land of Abyssinia according to some narrations. Various closely related narrations are mentioned, differing in brevity and detail, in sequence, in additions, and in identification; the most authentic of them is what Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from Suhayb that the Prophet (ﷺ) narrated this story to his companions. There is nothing in what was narrated explicitly stating that the Prophet (ﷺ) related it as an explanation of this verse, and al-Tirmidhi included its hadith in the exegesis of Surat al-Buruj.

From Muqatil: those who set up the trenches were in three lands: in Najran, in Syria, and in Persia. As for those in Syria, it was "Antyanyus al-Rumi"; as for the one in Persia, it was "Bukhtanassar"; and the one in Najran was "Yusuf dhu Nuwas." Let us mention the story which the Qur'an alluded to, taken from the biography of Ibn Ishaq, on the basis that it occurred in Najran in the land of Yemen. There was a king, who was Dhu Nuwas, who had a soothsayer or a sorcerer. The sorcerer had a disciple named 'Abd Allah ibn al-Thamir, who, when he walked to the soothsayer, would pass on his way a monastery in which was a monk who worshipped God according to the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and recited the Gospel, named "Fayminun," with fa', then ya', then mim, then ya' (it is vocalized in the European edition of the biography of Ibn Ishaq, which appears to have an original source vocalized as: fatha, then sukun, then kasra, then damma). Al-Suhayli said: al-Tabari has it with qaf instead of fa'. It may be distorted and said "Maymun," with mim at the beginning and one ya'. His origin was from Ghassan in Syria; then he wandered and settled in Najran, and he was isolated from people, secluded in his monastery. Miracles appeared to 'Abd Allah among his people, and whenever a miracle appeared to him, he invited those to whom it appeared to follow Christianity, so the Christians in Najran multiplied. This reached the king Dhu Nuwas, who was a Jew. The people of Najran were polytheists who worshipped a tall palm tree. So the king killed the boy and killed the monk, and ordered trenches to be made, into which wood was gathered and set ablaze, and the people of Najran were presented before it: whoever turned back from monotheism, he left alone, and whoever remained steadfast in the true religion, he threw into the fire.

So the companions of the trench were among those who were tormented from the people of the Christian faith in the land of the Arabs. Stories of trenches are numerous in history, and torment by burning is an ancient method, among them: the fire of Abraham (peace be upon him). As for the burning of 'Amr ibn Hind of a hundred men from the Banu Tamim and his being titled "al-Muharriq" (the Burner), I do not know that this was by means of making a trench. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: I saw in some books that the companions of the trench were al-Muharriq and his family, who burned a hundred men from the Banu Tamim.

The trench (al-Ukhdud): it follows the pattern *ufʿūl*, a form that is rare in use and not systematic. Other examples of it include *ufḥūṣ* (a hollow scraped in the ground), derived from the verb *faḥaṣat al-qaṭāh* ("the sand-grouse scraped the ground") and *al-dajājah* ("the hen") when she searches the dirt for a spot in which to lay her eggs. Other examples are *usluwb* (a noun meaning "method" or "a line of palm trees") and *uqnūm* (a noun meaning "the origin or essence of a thing"). This pattern may also occur with the feminine *tāʾ* (ة), as in *ukrūmah*, *ujūbah*, *uṭrūḥah* and *uḍḥūkah*.

His words "the fire" (al-nār) are a substitute (badal) for "the trench" (al-ukhdud), a badal ishtimal (a substitute of inclusion) or a badal baʿḍ min kull (a substitute of part from whole), because what is meant by "the trench" is the pit together with what is in it.

Al-waqūd, with a fatḥah on the waw, is the name of what fire is kindled with, such as firewood, oil or the like.

The meaning of *dhāt al-waqūd* ("full of fuel") is that its flame is never extinguished, because it has fuel that is thrown into it whenever it begins to die down.

The phrase ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾ is connected to the verb "was killed" (quttila). That is, they were cursed, and God's anger fell upon them, at the time they sat beside the trench.

The pronoun "they" (hum) refers to the people of the trench, since the king attends the execution of his command along with his chiefs, or it refers to those who were ordered by the king. According to the possibility that they were the king's helpers, "sitting" (quʿūd) means remaining close to the trench, which is expressed by sitting, so that those who stoke the fire do not become lax in keeping it burning. The preposition ʿalā (on/over) is used in its figurative sense of "over", because they did not sit above the fire but around it. The sense of nearness and watchfulness is expressed by the sense of "over", as in the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"The dew and the wind-blown one spent the night over the fire."

A similar usage is God's words ﴿he found upon it a community of people watering﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:23], meaning "beside it".

According to the possibility that "the people of the trench" refers to the believers who were tortured in it, then "sitting" is literal and ʿalā has its true sense of "on", meaning they were sitting on the fire, in that they were burning them while they were tied in the posture of sitting. That is because this is more severe in punishment and more humiliating. That is, after they had made them sit in the trenches, they lit the fire in them, and this is more awe-inspiring and more prolonged in punishment.

The pronoun "they" in His words ﴿and they are witnesses to what they do﴾ is repeated so that it is definitely understood to refer to some of the people of the trench.

The pronoun in "they do" may refer to "the people of the trench". The meaning of their being witnesses to what they do is that some of them bear witness for others before the king that none of them neglected what he had been charged with of burning the believers. Thus the plural pronouns and forms are distributed among different groups.

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to what the context implies, namely the division of the people of the trench into rulers and subordinates, which is characteristic of great undertakings. So when He reported about the people of the trench that they were sitting over the fire, it was understood that they were the ones charged with supervising the workers. Thus it is understood that they had followers, from stokers and guards, and so they are the referent of the pronoun in "they do".

On this interpretation, "witnesses" (shuhūd) may be the plural of *shāhid* in the sense of one who reports a truth, or it may mean one who is present and observing, since it is evident that no one bears witness regarding his own action.

The clause ﴿and they are witnesses to what they do to the believers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾, as if it was said: "sitting, witnessing their action against the believers", according to the two possibilities mentioned above regarding the referent of the pronoun "they do". The benefit of this circumstantial clause is to make that sitting appear more horrifying and to magnify its crime, since they were watching the torture of the believers without showing any mercy or recoiling from it. By this, the content of this clause differs from the content of the clause ﴿when they were sitting around it﴾, in terms of the connection of His words ﴿witnesses to the believers﴾.

The use of the relative pronoun in His words ﴿what they do to the believers﴾ contains an ambiguity that conveys that the stokers of the fire, the guards, the workers and those who directly throw the believers into it displayed harshness and cruelty in torturing the believers, in humiliating them and in mutilating them, and this goes beyond burning.

(p. 244)

The clause ﴿and they sought nothing against them except that they believed in God﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The *wāw* is either the *wāw* of circumstance or a conjunctive *wāw* connecting it to the preceding circumstantial clause.

The intent is to express wonder at the injustice of the people of the trench, that they committed such atrocity, not for a crime that would justify taking vengeance against its perpetrator. If those who dug the trench were Jews, as was the majority of the people of Yemen at that time, then the statement is a form of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, that is, "they took vengeance on them for nothing that deserves vengeance, but rather because they believed in God alone, just as those whom they tortured believed in Him." The point of wonder is that King Dhū Nuwās and the people of Yemen were adherents of Judaism, so they believed in God alone and did not associate partners with Him. How then could they torture people who believed in God alone, like themselves?! This is similar to His words ﴿Say: O People of the Book, do you disapprove of us only because we believed in God and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:59]. If those who dug the trench were polytheists, then among the Arabs of Yemen there remained those who worshipped the sun. In that case the exception (istithnāʾ) is not from the emphasis of a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, because the nature of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite is that what resembles the opposite of the intended meaning should in reality be of the same kind as the intended meaning. Therefore that device is used to emphasize the intended meaning. What is here is not like that, because the king and his army did in truth take vengeance on them for believing in God, if the king was a polytheist.

The application of the three attributes to the Name of Majesty (Allāh), namely "the Almighty, the Praiseworthy, ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾", serves to further establish that what they took vengeance on them for is not something that deserves vengeance. Rather, He is worthy of being praised for it, since they believed in a Lord who is worthy of being believed in, on account of His attributes which require that He alone be worshipped and that whatever is other than Him be rejected. For He supports His allies and rewards them, and He owns them. Whatever is other than Him is weak in might, neither harms nor benefits, and owns nothing of them, so the wonder at them is intensified by this.

The clause ﴿and God is witness over everything﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) containing a threat to those who made the trench and a promise to those who were tortured for the sake of God. It is also a threat to the likes of those disbelievers of Quraysh and others, to everyone who confronted the believers to harm them, and a promise to the Muslims who were tortured by the polytheists, such as Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb and Sumayyah.

[p. 245]

﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent will have the punishment of Hell, and they will have the punishment of the Burning.﴾

If this is the answer to the oath, according to some exegetes as mentioned earlier, then what lies between the oath and this statement is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridan) intended as a preparation (tawti'a) for threatening them with punishment and destruction, by mentioning what was promised to their counterparts.

If the answer is in His saying, ﴿The companions of the trench were destroyed﴾ [al-Buruj: 4], then His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believers﴾ is in the position of a summary (fadhlaka) of what He swore by, since the purpose of the oath and what it is sworn upon is the threatening of those among the polytheists of Quraysh who persecuted the believing men and women.

The emphasis of the statement with inna (indeed) is to refute the polytheists who deny that they bear any responsibility for persecuting the believers.

Those who persecuted the believing men and women are the polytheists of Quraysh, and the intended meaning is not the companions of the trench, because this does not fit His saying, ﴿then they did not repent﴾, since that is an allusion encouraging repentance, nor does it fit the entry of the fa' (so) into the predicate of inna in His saying, ﴿so for them is the punishment of Hell﴾, as will come.

Among those counted as persecutors of the believers were Abu Jahl, the head of the persecution and the one who kindled it; Umayyah ibn Khalaf; Safwan ibn Umayyah; al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth; al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; Umm Anmar; and a man from the Banu Taym.

As for the persecuted, among them were counted Bilal ibn Rabah, who was a slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and he used to torture him; Abu Fukayhah, who was a slave of Safwan ibn Umayyah; Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who was a slave of Umm Anmar; 'Ammar ibn Yasir, his father Yasir, and his brother 'Abd Allah, who were slaves of Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah, who assigned Abu Jahl to them; and 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah, who was a slave of a man from the Banu Taym.

Among the believing women who were persecuted: Hamamah, the mother of Bilal, a slave-woman of Umayyah ibn Khalaf; Zinnirah; Umm 'Unays, who was a slave-woman of al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth; al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, who were owned by al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; Latifah; Libinah, daughter of Fuhayrah, who belonged to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab before he embraced Islam, and 'Umar used to beat her; and Sumayyah, the mother of 'Ammar ibn Yasir, who belonged to the paternal uncle of Abu Jahl.

[p. 246]

Among those who were tried and returned to polytheism were al-Harith ibn Rabi'ah ibn al-Aswad, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, 'Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn al-Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj.

The specific mention of the believing women (atf al-mu'minat) serves to draw attention to their status, lest it be thought that this distinction belongs only to men, and to increase the enormity of the act of the persecutors, in that they transgressed against women, when it is proper that women not be treated harshly.

The clause ﴿then they did not repent﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah). Here thumma (then) indicates a delay of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because persisting in disbelief is greater than persecuting the believers.

In it there is an allusion to the polytheists that if they repent and believe, they will be spared the punishment of Hell.

Al-fatn (persecution) means treating someone with severity and placing them in hardship from which they cannot find escape except through hardship, a lesser harm, or a stratagem. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿And persecution is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The entry of the fa' (so) into the predicate of inna, in His saying, ﴿so for them is the punishment of Hell﴾, is because the subject of inna came as a relative clause (mawsul), and a relative clause is frequently understood in usage as containing the meaning of a conditional. So the implied sense is: indeed, those who persecuted the believers, then if they do not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell; because the conjoining of His saying, ﴿then they did not repent﴾ is intended to convey the meaning of restriction, so it functions like a condition.

The clause ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ is conjoined in the sense of verbal emphasis (al-ta'kid al-lafzi) of the clause ﴿for them is the punishment of Hell﴾. Its conjunction with the conjunction wa (and) is for the sake of intensifying the emphasis, by giving the impression that whoever wants to increase their threat with another warning will find nothing greater than the first warning. Yet there is a difference in meaning between the punishment of Hell and the punishment of the Burning, although the outcome of the two meanings is one. This kind of difference justifies the conjunction of emphasis.

Moreover, casting them into Hell is itself a punishment before they taste the punishment of its burning, because of the disgrace in it and being driven forcefully along their way. He, exalted is He, said, ﴿On the Day they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent push﴾ [al-Tur: 13]. Thus through this there arises a difference between the two clauses.

It is also permissible that by the second be meant the multiplication of the punishment for them, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God—We will increase their punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

[p. 247]

It is also permissible that by the punishment of the Burning be meant a burning other than Hell, namely a fire of torment kindled upon them before the Day of Reckoning, as came in the hadith: "The grave is a pit from the pits of Hell or a garden from the gardens of Paradise." Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan from Ibn 'Umar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 85, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great triumph.﴾

It is permissible that this be a explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani) arising from His saying: ﴿Then they did not repent﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], which implies that if they had repented, there would have been for them no punishment of Hell. So the listener becomes eager to know their state: is it limited to safety from the punishment of Hell, or is it above that? Thus he is informed that for them are gardens, for repentance is faith. Therefore the relative clause "those who believed" was used instead of "those who repented," to indicate that faith and righteous deeds constitute the repentance from polytheism that incited the persecution of the believers. This resumptive sentence came as an interjection (i'tiraD).

It is also permissible that it be an interjection (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10] and the clause ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj: 12], an interjection of good tidings amid the warning, to encourage those being warned toward faith, and to strengthen the believers in what they endure of the harm of the polytheists, according to the Qur'an's custom of following intimidation with encouragement.

The emphasis with "inna" is for the importance of the news.

The demonstrative "dhalika" refers to what was mentioned of their being singled out for the gardens and rivers.

And "al-kabir" (the great) is used figuratively for what is intense in its domain, and "al-fawz" (the triumph) is a verbal noun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 85, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe.﴾

The clause ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe﴾ is a reason (ʿilla) for the content of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10] up to His saying: ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Buruj: 10]. That is, because the seizing of God is severe upon those who persecuted those who believed in Him. Thus the placement of ʾinna (indeed) in the sense of causation makes the particle of causation (fa' al-tasabbub) unnecessary.

Page 248
The seizing of God includes His punishment of them in Hell, and it includes what precedes that of what occurs in the Hereafter and what occurs in this world. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The day We seize with the greatest seizing, indeed We will be avengers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]. The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), because the seizing of God against those who persecuted the believers contains victory for the Prophet (ﷺ) and steadfastness for him.

**Translation:**

It is suitable that it be a fresh, independent resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), shifting from their threat with the punishment of the Hereafter to their threat with a punishment in this world that comes from the seizing (*batsh*) of God. He followed it with the threat of the punishment of the Hereafter, because it strikes harder into the hearts of the polytheists, since they think they are safe from punishment, as they do not believe in the Resurrection, and so they reckon that they have won the good of the life of this world.

The meaning is that God seizes them in the beginning and in the return, that is, in this world and in the Hereafter.

It is also suitable that it be a justification (*ta'lil*) for the sentence ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj: 12], because He who originates and restores is able to inflict severe seizing in this world, which is the origination, and in the Hereafter, which is the restoring of the seizing.

It is also suitable that it be an incorporation (*idmaj*, a proof woven into the discourse) of an argument for the possibility of the Resurrection, meaning that God originates creation and then restores it, and this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

The *batsh* is taking by force and severity, and it is used metaphorically for painful, severe punishment, as it is here.

*Yubdi'* is a synonym of *yabda'*; one says *bada'a* and *abda'a*. So the *hamza* in *abda'a* is not for transitivity (*ta'diyah*).

The two verbs' objects are omitted in order to intend the generality of what the two verbs apply to, of everything that occurs initially and is then repeated. It thus includes the beginning of creation and its restoration, which is the Resurrection; it includes the first seizing in this world and the seizing in the Hereafter; and it includes the bringing into being of generations and their succession after the destruction of earlier ones. Within these considerations there are many implications of threat for the polytheists.

The separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) in His saying *wa-huwa yubdi'* is for emphasis, that is, for confirming the predicate, and there is no place for restriction (*qasr*) here, since in this context there is no refutation of anyone who claims that other than God originates and restores. This has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah, that the separating pronoun is followed by the present-tense verb according to the view of al-Mazini, and this is for confirmation (*tahqiq*). Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And the plotting of those—it will perish﴾ [Fatir: 10], which has been discussed in Surat Fatir.

[Page 249]

[Page 250]

This sentence is coordinated with the sentence "Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe" (Al-Buruj: 12), and its content is a counterpart to the content of that sentence. Since it was stated that the content of the sentence "Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and women" (Al-Buruj: 10) and what follows is a cause, it was fitting that it be matched by a cause for the content of the sentence "Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds will have gardens" (Al-Buruj: 11) and what follows. So it was given as a cause by His saying, ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving﴾. He forgives those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds the sins they committed, and He loves the repentant and holds affection for them.

Al-Wadud is on the pattern fa'ul in the sense of fa'il, derived from al-wudd, which is love. So the meaning of al-Wadud is the one who loves, and it is one of His names, Exalted is He. That is, He loves His creatures as long as they do not turn away from His commandment.
