The address is to an unspecified person among the polytheists whom one wishes to admonish, as an implicit reference (kinaya) to reminding them of their history. This is because the condition of those who engage in conduct like theirs, persisting stubbornly in obstinacy, is like the condition of one who does not know their story, so he is asked whether news of them has reached him or not. Alternatively, it is an address to an unspecified person in order to express wonder at the polytheists' condition in turning away from taking warning from this. In that case the interrogative is used to express wonder (ta'ajjub).

Al-ita' (the coming) is used metaphorically (isti'arah) for the reaching of news, and al-hadith means the news. This was discussed earlier in Surat al-Nazi'at.

Al-junud (the armies) is the plural of jund, which is a military force gathered for fighting. It is applied to the peoples who gathered to oppose the messengers, as in His words: ﴿A host of confederates, routed there﴾ [Sad: 11]. The word jund was also used metaphorically for the chiefs (al-mala'), by His words: ﴿And the chiefs among them set off﴾ [Sad: 6]. Then the metaphor was reinforced (tarshih) by the metaphor "routed" (mahzum), which means defeated in war, and it was used for those who are destroyed and uprooted without any war.

Fir'awn and Thamud are in apposition (badal mutabiq) to al-junud, a full apposition, because the purpose is to take a lesson from these two.

Fir'awn is the name of the king of Egypt from the Copts. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-A'raf: 103], in Surat al-A'raf.

The expression is elliptical, with an omitted modifier (mudaf mahdhuf), because Fir'awn is not an army, but the army is attributed to him: the armies who denied Moses, peace be upon him, and harmed him. The modifier was omitted for the rhetorical purpose of pairing (muzawajah) between two single proper names in the apposition to al-junud.

They opposed him because he called to the worship of the true Lord, and that angered Pharaoh, who claimed that he was the god of the Copts and the son of their gods.

The mention of Thamud, among the other nations that denied the messengers, is singled out from among the Arab peoples such as 'Ad and the people of Tubba', and from others such as the people of Noah and the people of Shu'ayb. This is because the closing rhyme (fasilah) required it, the seventh verse-ending that runs on the letter dal in His words: ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj: 12]. Since this name fitted the rhyme and its mention involved no artificiality, choosing it is among the excellences of the composition of speech.

The mention of Thamud was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿And to Thamud their brother Salih﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], in Surat al-A'raf. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 85, verse 19–20:

Page 252
﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in denial.﴾ ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind.﴾

This is a transitional "nay" (idrab intiqali) turning to their aversion to taking heed from the state of the nations who denied the messengers. It means that they are persistent in denial and immersed in it, immersed like the contained in the container, so the firm settling of denial in their souls is made like the firm settling of the container around the contained.

In this there is an indication that the encompassing of denial around them is like the encompassing of the container around the contained, which leaves no path for their minds to reflect upon what befell the likes of them among the nations. For this reason He did not say "those who disbelieve are denying" as He said in Surah al-Inshiqaq.

The object of the denial is omitted because it is evident from the context. The implied sense is: they are in denial of the Prophet ﷺ, of the revelation sent down to him, and of the Resurrection.

The clause ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind﴾ is conjoined (atf) to the clause ﴿Those who disbelieve are in denial﴾, meaning: they are firmly settled in denial, while Allah is imposing upon them a punishment from which they cannot escape. So His saying ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind﴾ is an analogy for the state of the punishment awaiting them while they are heedless of it, to the state of one whom an enemy has encircled from behind while he does not know; until, when he attempts to flee and escape, he finds the enemy encompassing him. The intended meaning here is not the encompassing of Allah's knowledge of their denial, for that would be of little benefit.

The recompense of the encompassing of denial around them has been matched with the encompassing of punishment around them, as a fitting requital. Thus His saying ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind﴾ is a statement used in the sense of warning and threat.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 85, verses 21–22:**

﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a preserved tablet﴾.

This is an *idrab* (a turning away from the previous statement) that serves to refute their denial. The Qur'an came to them with clear proofs, so their persistence in denial results from their corrupt belief in the truthfulness of the Qur'an. They described it with defects, saying: "Tales of the ancients" (*asatir al-awwalin*), "a fabricated lie" (*ifk mufta*), "the saying of a soothsayer" (*qawl kahin*), and "the saying of a poet" (*qawl sha'ir*). So praising it (*tanwih*) by these words comprehensively refutes all their trivialities, by way of concision (*ijaz*).

[Page 253]

*Qur'an* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *qari'a*, on the pattern *fu'lan*, which denotes abundance of meaning, like *shukran* and *qurban*. It derives from *al-qira'a*, which is the recitation of a speech that was uttered at an earlier time than the time of its reciter's recitation, in the same form as its speaker uttered it, whether it was written in a page or was taught by heart to the reciter, such that the reciter's speech does not differ from its original. For this reason, the transmission of a speech is not called *qira'a* unless the speech is written or preserved.

Whenever *qur'an* appears indefinite, it is a verbal noun. As for the name of the Book of Islam, it is with the definite article *al-*, because it is a proper name by predominance (*'alam bil-ghalaba*).

Thus, naming the revelation sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) as "Qur'an" is a conventional indication that it is revealed, an implicit (*ta'rid*) refutation of what the deniers invented: that it is "tales of the ancients" or "the saying of a soothsayer," or the like.

It is described with another attribute: that it is deposited in a tablet (*lawh*).

A *lawh* is a flat piece of wood made to be written upon.

The placement of the description *fi lawh* in the context of praising the Qur'an and the tablet specifies that the tablet is a sacred existent from among the beings of the exalted, unseen world. The verse says no more than that the tablet contains the Qur'an. God made the Qur'an written in an exalted tablet, just as He made the Torah written in tablets and gave them to Moses (peace be upon him), saying: "And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything" (7:145), and He said: "And he threw down the tablets" (7:150), and He said: "When the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets" (7:154). As for the tablet of the Qur'an, He made it preserved in the exalted world.

Some scholars of kalam (theology) interpreted the tablet as an existent in which all created things are recorded collectively and in summary. They named this the "Clear Book" (*al-kitab al-mubin*), they named the recording of created things in it *qada'* (decree), and they named their manifestation in existence *qadar* (measure). Al-Isfahani followed this in his commentary on *al-Tawali'*, as transmitted by al-Manjur in his commentary on Ibn Zakari's poem, presented in the section of transmitted doctrines (*al-'aqa'id al-sam'iyya*). In that there is consideration. Traditions of varying strength report that Israfil is entrusted with it, and that it is located to the right of the Throne. This verse implies that the entire Qur'an is recorded in it.

[Page 254]

In the verses of Surah al-Waqi'a occurs: "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" (56:77), "in a Book well-guarded" (56:78). This is apparent in that the Preserved Tablet and the Well-Guarded Book are one and the same thing.

As for *mahfuz* (preserved) and *maknun* (well-guarded), there is a difference between them in concept, and a partial overlap (*'umum wa khusus wajhi*) in their occurrence. *Mahfuz* means protected from everything that would damage or diminish it and that is unfitting for it, and that is a perfection for it. *Maknun* means that which is not permitted to be touched by everyone, owing to concern for it because of its preciousness. No authentic hadith has been established concerning the tablet or its specific properties, and everything said about it consists of statements attributed to some of the early generation (*salaf*), whose chains of attribution are not known.

It is reported that the pen was the first thing God created, and He said to it: "Write," so it ran with what would be until eternity. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, and al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib," and in it (there is a narration) from Ibn 'Abbas. End of quotation.

The creation of the pen does not indicate the creation of the tablet, because the pen writes on the tablet and on other than it.

*Al-majid* means great in its kind, as has preceded in His saying: "Lord of the Throne, the Glorious" (85:15). The Qur'an is called *majid* because it is the greatest of the heavenly books, and the most abundant in meanings, guidance and admonition, and it surpasses them with its eloquence, its rhetorical excellence, and its inimitability (*i'jaz*), which renders humans unable to produce its like.

It occurs in al-Sayyid al-Jurjani's *al-Ta'rifat* that there are four tablets.

The first: the Tablet of Decree, prior to erasure and affirmation, and it is the Tablet of the First Intellect.

The second: the Tablet of Measure, that is, the Universal Rational Soul, and it is what is called the Preserved Tablet.

The third: the Tablet of the Particular Celestial Soul, in which everything in this world is imprinted with its form, its configuration and its measure, and it is what is called the Lowest Heaven.

The fourth: the Tablet of Matter (*al-hayula*), receptive to form in the world of witnessing. End of quotation.

This is a terminology mixed between Sufism and philosophy, and perhaps it is something al-Sayyid extrapolated from the words of several scholars.

[Page 255]

The majority (*al-jumhur*) read *mahfuzin* with the genitive (*jarr*), as an attribute of *lawh*. The preservation of the tablet in which the Qur'an is found is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the preservation of the Qur'an.

Nafi' alone read *mahfuzun* with the nominative (*raf'*), as a second attribute of *Qur'an*, and the phrase *fi lawh* is connected to *mahfuz*. The preservation of the Qur'an necessitates that the tablet in which it is deposited is also preserved. Therefore, from the two readings there resulted the affirmation of preservation for both the Qur'an and the tablet. As for the preservation of the Qur'an, it is its protection from alteration and from being snatched by devils. God, exalted, said: "Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians" (15:9).

As for the Preserved Tablet, it is its protection from being touched by other than the angels, or its preservation is a metonymy for its sanctification, like His saying, exalted: "In a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified" (56:78–79).

Surah al-Tariq

Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated from Abu Hurayra: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite in the late evening prayer (*al-'isha' al-akhira*) 'By the heaven with the constellations' and 'By the heaven and the night-comer'." End of quotation. So Abu Hurayra named it "(Surat) al-Sama' wal-Tariq," because the more apparent view is that the *waw* in His saying "By the heaven and the night-comer" (86:1) is the *waw* of conjunction, and for this reason the first verse of it was not mentioned; rather, a name was taken for it from the wording of the verse, just as he said regarding "the heaven with the constellations" (85:1).

It is called in the books of tafsir, the books of Sunna, and in the mushafs "Surat al-Tariq," because this word occurs at its beginning. In Tafsir al-Tabari and Ahkam Ibn al-'Arabi, it is titled "(Wal-Sama'i wal-Tariq)."

It has seventeen verses.

It is Meccan by consensus; it was revealed before the tenth year of the Prophethood. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 85, verses 21–22:**

﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a preserved tablet﴾.

This is an *idrab* (a turning away from the previous statement) that serves to refute their denial. The Qur'an came to them with clear proofs, so their persistence in denial results from their corrupt belief in the truthfulness of the Qur'an. They described it with defects, saying: "Tales of the ancients" (*asatir al-awwalin*), "a fabricated lie" (*ifk mufta*), "the saying of a soothsayer" (*qawl kahin*), and "the saying of a poet" (*qawl sha'ir*). So praising it (*tanwih*) by these words comprehensively refutes all their trivialities, by way of concision (*ijaz*).

[Page 253]

*Qur'an* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *qari'a*, on the pattern *fu'lan*, which denotes abundance of meaning, like *shukran* and *qurban*. It derives from *al-qira'a*, which is the recitation of a speech that was uttered at an earlier time than the time of its reciter's recitation, in the same form as its speaker uttered it, whether it was written in a page or was taught by heart to the reciter, such that the reciter's speech does not differ from its original. For this reason, the transmission of a speech is not called *qira'a* unless the speech is written or preserved.

Whenever *qur'an* appears indefinite, it is a verbal noun. As for the name of the Book of Islam, it is with the definite article *al-*, because it is a proper name by predominance (*'alam bil-ghalaba*).

Thus, naming the revelation sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) as "Qur'an" is a conventional indication that it is revealed, an implicit (*ta'rid*) refutation of what the deniers invented: that it is "tales of the ancients" or "the saying of a soothsayer," or the like.

It is described with another attribute: that it is deposited in a tablet (*lawh*).

A *lawh* is a flat piece of wood made to be written upon.

The placement of the description *fi lawh* in the context of praising the Qur'an and the tablet specifies that the tablet is a sacred existent from among the beings of the exalted, unseen world. The verse says no more than that the tablet contains the Qur'an. God made the Qur'an written in an exalted tablet, just as He made the Torah written in tablets and gave them to Moses (peace be upon him), saying: "And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything" (7:145), and He said: "And he threw down the tablets" (7:150), and He said: "When the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets" (7:154). As for the tablet of the Qur'an, He made it preserved in the exalted world.

Some scholars of kalam (theology) interpreted the tablet as an existent in which all created things are recorded collectively and in summary. They named this the "Clear Book" (*al-kitab al-mubin*), they named the recording of created things in it *qada'* (decree), and they named their manifestation in existence *qadar* (measure). Al-Isfahani followed this in his commentary on *al-Tawali'*, as transmitted by al-Manjur in his commentary on Ibn Zakari's poem, presented in the section of transmitted doctrines (*al-'aqa'id al-sam'iyya*). In that there is consideration. Traditions of varying strength report that Israfil is entrusted with it, and that it is located to the right of the Throne. This verse implies that the entire Qur'an is recorded in it.

[Page 254]

In the verses of Surah al-Waqi'a occurs: "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" (56:77), "in a Book well-guarded" (56:78). This is apparent in that the Preserved Tablet and the Well-Guarded Book are one and the same thing.

As for *mahfuz* (preserved) and *maknun* (well-guarded), there is a difference between them in concept, and a partial overlap (*'umum wa khusus wajhi*) in their occurrence. *Mahfuz* means protected from everything that would damage or diminish it and that is unfitting for it, and that is a perfection for it. *Maknun* means that which is not permitted to be touched by everyone, owing to concern for it because of its preciousness. No authentic hadith has been established concerning the tablet or its specific properties, and everything said about it consists of statements attributed to some of the early generation (*salaf*), whose chains of attribution are not known.

It is reported that the pen was the first thing God created, and He said to it: "Write," so it ran with what would be until eternity. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, and al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib," and in it (there is a narration) from Ibn 'Abbas. End of quotation.

The creation of the pen does not indicate the creation of the tablet, because the pen writes on the tablet and on other than it.

*Al-majid* means great in its kind, as has preceded in His saying: "Lord of the Throne, the Glorious" (85:15). The Qur'an is called *majid* because it is the greatest of the heavenly books, and the most abundant in meanings, guidance and admonition, and it surpasses them with its eloquence, its rhetorical excellence, and its inimitability (*i'jaz*), which renders humans unable to produce its like.

It occurs in al-Sayyid al-Jurjani's *al-Ta'rifat* that there are four tablets.

The first: the Tablet of Decree, prior to erasure and affirmation, and it is the Tablet of the First Intellect.

The second: the Tablet of Measure, that is, the Universal Rational Soul, and it is what is called the Preserved Tablet.

The third: the Tablet of the Particular Celestial Soul, in which everything in this world is imprinted with its form, its configuration and its measure, and it is what is called the Lowest Heaven.

The fourth: the Tablet of Matter (*al-hayula*), receptive to form in the world of witnessing. End of quotation.

This is a terminology mixed between Sufism and philosophy, and perhaps it is something al-Sayyid extrapolated from the words of several scholars.

The majority (*al-jumhur*) read *mahfuzin* with the genitive (*jarr*), as an attribute of *lawh*. The preservation of the tablet in which the Qur'an is found is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the preservation of the Qur'an.

Nafi' alone read *mahfuzun* with the nominative (*raf'*), as a second attribute of *Qur'an*, and the phrase *fi lawh* is connected to *mahfuz*. The preservation of the Qur'an necessitates that the tablet in which it is deposited is also preserved. Therefore, from the two readings there resulted the affirmation of preservation for both the Qur'an and the tablet. As for the preservation of the Qur'an, it is its protection from alteration and from being snatched by devils. God, exalted, said: "Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians" (15:9).

As for the Preserved Tablet, it is its protection from being touched by other than the angels, or its preservation is a metonymy for its sanctification, like His saying, exalted: "In a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified" (56:78–79).
